Who the Babylonian king was occupies four voices with four kinds of evidence. Gill runs through inherited identifications, rejecting the one that made him Nebuchadnezzar's father and the one that made him Esarhaddon, who ruled Assyria and not Babylon, and settles on the Mardocempad of the astronomical canon. Ellicott works from the Assyrian inscriptions, where the man is conspicuous as a rebel against Sargon who set up an independent monarchy and is styled son of Yakin, which he takes for a dynastic appellative, as an Israelite king is called son of Omri in the same records. Keil and Delitzsch give the fullest account from those monuments: a vassal for twelve years, a rebel twice over, and at last a refugee on an island in the Persian Gulf. Calvin, without the inscriptions, makes him the first of his nation to bear the royal title and adds that he subdued the Assyrians, so it is a mistake to date that war from Nebuchadnezzar.

What the embassy wanted divides them more sharply. Henry takes the friendly reading first, that civility teaches men to rejoice with those who rejoice and that if Christians are unneighbourly the heathen will shame them; then turns it, since the court was made to Hezekiah not because he was pious but because he was prosperous. Ellicott allows the two ostensible objects, congratulation and enquiry about the sign on the dial, but believes the real business was an alliance, the present reading in eastern terms almost like an acknowledgment of Hezekiah's leadership. Calvin makes it craft throughout, and adds a subtler point: the heathen had heard of the miracle and reckoned an ally so visibly favoured would carry the war under heaven's protection.

Clarke leaves the history to the others and works the text. He judges that the parallel account in the earlier book has hitherto been the more correct, but that here the advantage lies with this chapter, from which two of its words should be corrected. He also argues that a word for ambassadors has dropped out of both Hebrew copies, since the Greek supplies it and the narration afterwards refers to the men as though they had been named already.

On what Hezekiah did wrong they converge. Gill says he was glad not of the presents, being rich and not covetous, but of the honour, and names two sins, vain glory and the vain confidence of trusting an arm of flesh. Calvin states the difficulty plainly: anyone barely reading would conclude the king did nothing wrong, since it was humanity to receive the men cheerfully and barbarous to spurn them, yet ostentation lurked in the heart, and he had turned to foreign aid from one lately his deliverer twice over. Ellicott reads the display as political rather than vain, a showing of the kingdom's resources to impress the ambassadors with his worth as an ally, and uses the treasures to date the embassy before the payment to the Assyrian.

The prophet comes unsent for, and Gill and Calvin both press that Hezekiah had sent for him readily while ill and forgot him in prosperity, Calvin adding that prophets are sought in distress and despised in ease because they disturb our mirth. Ellicott hears in the questions the authority of age and of a divine commission, perhaps of a master addressing a former pupil. The answer about the far country divides them: Ellicott takes it for a plea, since men who had travelled so far in his honour could hardly be refused and a distant land seemed free of the danger of the Egyptian alliance; Calvin takes it for a boast, the prophet knowing the country well enough without such magnificent language. Calvin observes that the king then answers modestly and confesses the fact without yet acknowledging the sin, so drugged by an ambition that intoxicates and then maddens.
5:
Gill notes that only now does the prophet own that he came from the Lord with a rebuke. Calvin argues backwards from the severity: since God observes the highest moderation in chastising, so heavy a punishment proves the fault no ordinary one, and men judge amiss where God alone is competent. He then sets out the apologies and dismisses them: were the treasures heaped up to lie hidden in the earth for ever, should the messengers have been driven away, ought the friendship of a rival to Assyria to have been rejected? So far as appearances go, nothing here is without an apology. What God sees instead is ingratitude, pride, an appetite for a ruinous alliance, and above all ambition; whence he quotes the exclamation that the poison of pride is so great it can be cured only by poison, the thorn given to an apostle being the cure meant.

Henry reads the punishment as retributive: it is just with God to take from us what we make the matter of our pride, and the king who displayed his treasure acted like a foolish traveller showing his money to one who proves a thief; the Babylon that courted Jerusalem in due course conquered her, which is what leagues with irreligious men come to. Gill finds mercy mixed into the justice, since time was given, and expects fulfilment within a few reigns, where Clarke reckons it a hundred and fifty years off and calls the interval a proof of divine omniscience. On the sons Gill notes that the immediate heir was taken and released and does not appear to have been made a eunuch, so the words found their fulfilment in a later king and his children.

Calvin raises against himself the objection that a city's sack and a nation's captivity cannot justly be charged to one man, since scripture elsewhere lays them to the people's general obstinacy. There is no absurdity, he answers, in God punishing at once one man's sin and a whole nation's crimes: when wrath overspreads a country it is the duty of each to consider what he has deserved, so that no man throws the blame on others. He cites the numbering of the people, where the anger of the Lord was kindled against the nation first and the king's act followed.

The king's reply divides the tile five ways. Gill takes it for immediate repentance, the sin acknowledged and the sentence owned just. Henry allows a reasonable contentment: we must not be regardless of those who come after, yet may reckon ourselves well done by if there is peace and truth in our days, and count it a favour to reach harbour before the storm. Ellicott is severe: the words have the appearance of pious resignation, but are less true and noble than the king's who said of a like sentence, I have sinned, but these sheep, what have they done; and this thanksgiving reminds him too much of the saying that after him may come the flood. Clarke rescues the king by reading the sentence as a question, whether there shall be prosperity in his days and whether he shall escape the evil foretold, since understood otherwise the words show a pitiful unconcern for his family and nation.

Calvin holds the received reading. The particle marks an exception, so the king adds something new and gives thanks for a mitigation: God might have raised up enemies at once, and by delaying has moderated what was deserved. He meets the charge of cruelty toward posterity, calling the sayings that wish the earth burnt once a man is dead profane and the property of swine and Epicureans, and insisting this is different, since the king wished well to those after him but could not disregard a token of forbearance. Ellicott adds that the second word of the promise means stability.
